options.why: CloudFront retries the secondary origin per request when the primary returns the configured error codes, with no DNS change.

options.text: Add a Lambda@Edge function that rewrites requests to the us-west-2 bucket when it detects errors.
options.why: Custom code for a feature CloudFront provides natively.

options.text: Use an S3 Multi-Region Access Point as the origin with failover controls.
options.why: Multi-Region Access Points can fail over, but failover controls are a manual active/passive switch; origin groups react per request automatically.

questions.explain: CloudFront origin groups give automatic per-request origin failover for chosen status codes. Combined with S3 replication, they are the simplest highly available static origin.

questions.stem: A media monitoring company runs 300 EC2 instances that were sized two years ago by guesswork. Finance suspects many are oversized but the team does not know which ones or what size to choose, and it wants recommendations based on actual usage rather than a manual review. Which service should the solutions architect use?

options.text: AWS Compute Optimizer.
options.why: Compute Optimizer analyses CloudWatch utilization history and recommends right-sized instance types for EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS, Lambda and ECS on Fargate.

options.text: AWS Budgets with a monthly cost threshold.
options.why: Budgets alert on spending but don't say which instances are oversized.

options.text: Amazon Inspector.
options.why: Inspector finds vulnerabilities, not sizing problems.

options.text: AWS Cost and Usage Report queried with Athena.
options.why: The CUR shows what you spent, but not CPU or memory use, so it can't recommend a size by itself.

questions.explain: Right-sizing starts with Compute Optimizer, which uses metrics. Cost Explorer, CUR and Budgets show spend; Trusted Advisor gives broader checks. Enable memory metrics through the CloudWatch agent for better EC2 recommendations.

questions.stem: An online publisher must prove to auditors that it records API activity from every AWS account in its organization, including accounts created in future, and that delivered log files have not been changed afterwards. Member account administrators must not be able to stop the logging. Which actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an organization trail from the management account that delivers to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log-archive account.
options.why: An organization trail covers all member accounts, including new ones, and member accounts cannot modify or delete it.

options.text: Enable CloudTrail log file integrity validation on the trail.
options.why: CloudTrail writes signed digest files, so you can prove whether a log file was changed or deleted after delivery.

options.text: Rely on CloudTrail event history in each account.
options.why: Event history keeps only 90 days of management events per account and cannot prove integrity.

options.text: Enable CloudTrail Insights on each account's trail.
options.why: Insights detects unusual API call volume; it neither centralizes logs nor proves they weren't altered.

options.text: Deploy an AWS Config conformance pack that checks that CloudTrail is enabled.
options.why: Config can report that logging was turned off, but it does not prevent it or validate log files.

questions.explain: Central, tamper-evident audit logging is an organization trail into a separate log-archive account plus log file validation. Detective checks such as Config tell you what broke; they don't keep the record.

questions.stem: A digital magazine shows a live 'most read in the last hour' list on every page. It is built by a SQL query over a 400-million-row page-view table in Aurora PostgreSQL that runs on each page load, and at 20,000 page views per second the database CPU is at 95%. The list may be up to a few seconds stale. Which solution provides the BEST performance?

options.text: Add Aurora Replicas and spread the ranking query across them.
options.why: It spreads the load, but the expensive aggregation still runs 20,000 times a second, and more replicas raise cost.

options.text: Create a materialized view of the ranking and refresh it every second.
options.why: Refreshing a large aggregation every second still loads the primary heavily.

options.text: Keep counts in an ElastiCache sorted set and read the top entries from it.
options.why: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score in memory, so increments and top-N reads take microseconds and the database no longer runs the query.

options.text: Export page views to S3 every minute and query the ranking with Athena.
options.why: Athena queries take seconds and cost money per scan, which is far too slow for every page load.

questions.explain: Real-time rankings, counters and leaderboards suit in-memory data structures such as Redis or Valkey sorted sets. Precompute the answer once rather than aggregating on every read.

questions.stem: A TV talent show lets viewers vote through a mobile app during a 10-minute window, peaking at 150,000 votes per second. Votes are written to an Amazon RDS database that handles about 5,000 writes per second, and it failed under load last season. Every vote must be counted, but results can be published 15 minutes after voting closes. Which design is MOST resilient?

options.text: Scale the RDS instance to the largest available class for the show.
options.why: Even the largest instance is unlikely to absorb 30 times its normal write rate, and a failure still loses votes.

options.text: Buffer votes in an SQS queue and let Lambda write them to the database in batches.
options.why: The queue accepts the burst durably, and consumers drain it within the 15 minutes using batching and limited concurrency.

options.text: Have API Gateway invoke a Lambda function that writes each vote through RDS Proxy.
options.why: RDS Proxy pools connections, but the database still receives 150,000 writes per second and fails.

options.text: Write votes to ElastiCache first and copy them to RDS when voting closes.
options.why: The cache absorbs writes, but a node failure before the copy could lose votes, so 'every vote counted' is not guaranteed without extra persistence settings.

questions.explain: When a write spike exceeds what the database can take and results can wait, put a queue in front of it: accept fast, persist durably, drain at the database's pace. Connection pooling doesn't reduce write volume.

questions.stem: A streaming company exposes an internal royalty-reporting API through Amazon API Gateway backed by Lambda. Finance tools that call it run in three VPCs in the same account and Region. The API contains revenue data, so it must not be reachable from the internet at all. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep the API regional and protect it with API keys and a usage plan.
options.why: API keys are for throttling and metering, not access control, and the API stays reachable from the internet.

options.text: Create a private REST API, add an execute-api interface VPC endpoint in each VPC, and use a resource policy that allows only those endpoints.
options.why: Private APIs are reachable only through interface VPC endpoints, and the resource policy limits which endpoints can call them.

options.text: Keep the API regional and attach an AWS WAF web ACL that allows only the NAT gateway IP addresses of the three VPCs.
options.why: It works as a filter, but the endpoint is still public and the allowlist breaks whenever NAT addresses change.

options.text: Replace API Gateway with Lambda function URLs that use the NONE auth type and keep the URLs known only to the finance tools.
options.why: Function URLs with NONE auth are public endpoints, the opposite of the requirement.

questions.explain: 'Not reachable from the internet' for API Gateway means a private REST API plus interface endpoints and a resource policy. Public endpoints with filters still face the internet.

questions.stem: A photo-sharing app creates five thumbnail sizes for every uploaded image and stores them in S3 Standard; together they total 180 TB. Thumbnails are read occasionally and can be regenerated from the originals, which are stored separately in S3 Standard. Losing some thumbnails in a rare AZ failure is acceptable. Which storage class is MOST cost-effective for the thumbnails?

options.text: S3 Standard-Infrequent Access.
options.why: It stores data across multiple AZs, which costs more than needed for data that can be regenerated.

options.text: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
options.why: Reads would need restores taking minutes to hours, which doesn't work for thumbnails shown in an app.

options.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
options.why: Its tiers store data across several AZs, objects under 128 KB are never moved to cheaper tiers, and larger ones add a per-object monitoring fee.

options.text: S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access.
options.why: One Zone-IA is about 20% cheaper than Standard-IA and fits infrequently read data that can be recreated if an AZ is lost.

questions.explain: One Zone-IA is for re-creatable, infrequently accessed data: derived copies, thumbnails, secondary backups. Durable originals stay in multi-AZ classes.

questions.stem: A media-measurement company keeps the last 13 months of audience data in an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster and 6 years of older Parquet data in S3. Analysts occasionally need a query that joins both. Loading the history into Redshift would triple the cluster size. Which solution meets this need with the LEAST effort?

options.text: Create external tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and query the S3 data in place with Amazon Redshift Spectrum, joining it with local tables.
options.why: Spectrum queries S3 data directly from Redshift SQL, so analysts can join history with warehouse tables without loading it.

options.text: Resize the cluster and COPY the 6 years of history into Redshift.
options.why: It works, but you pay for a much larger cluster to serve occasional queries.

options.text: Export the 13 months of Redshift data to S3 every night and run all queries in Athena.
options.why: It moves the whole warehouse workload to a new engine and a new pipeline, which is more effort and slower for daily dashboards.

options.text: Load the history into a separate Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database and join across databases in application code.
options.why: RDS is not built for multi-TB analytics, and joining in application code is slow and fragile.

questions.explain: Keep hot data in the warehouse and cold history in S3, and join them with Redshift Spectrum or federated queries. Separating storage from compute avoids sizing a cluster for rarely queried data.

questions.stem: A regional newspaper runs its nightly circulation report on a single EC2 instance using cron. The job takes 25 minutes and needs 4 GB of memory. Last month the instance's host failed, and nobody noticed that the report did not run for a week. The company wants the job to run on schedule without managing servers and to alert someone if it fails. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Move the cron entry to a second EC2 instance in another AZ as a backup.
options.why: Two servers to patch, and both could run the job or neither may notice the other's failure.

options.text: Rewrite the job as a Lambda function triggered by an EventBridge schedule.
options.why: Lambda's 15-minute maximum timeout is shorter than the 25-minute job.

options.text: Run it as a Fargate task from EventBridge Scheduler and alert through SNS on task failure.
options.why: Fargate runs long containers with no servers to manage, the schedule is managed and highly available, and failure events can trigger an alert.

options.text: Put the instance in an Auto Scaling group of one so that it is replaced on failure.
options.why: Self-healing helps, but it still means managing a server, and a replacement does not rerun the missed job or alert anyone.

questions.explain: Scheduled jobs belong to a managed scheduler (EventBridge Scheduler) plus serverless compute that fits the runtime: Lambda up to 15 minutes, Fargate or AWS Batch beyond. Add failure events so that silence is never success.

questions.stem: An ad-insertion company runs its service behind a Network Load Balancer in its own VPC. Forty broadcaster customers want to call the service privately from their own VPCs in other AWS accounts. Many customers use 10.0.0.0/16, the same range as the provider's VPC. Customers must not gain access to anything else in the provider's network. Which solution is MOST secure?

options.text: Create VPC peering connections between the provider VPC and each customer VPC.
options.why: Peering cannot connect VPCs with overlapping CIDR blocks, and it opens routing to the whole VPC rather than one service.

options.text: Attach all VPCs to a shared AWS Transit Gateway with a route table per customer.
options.why: Transit Gateway also needs non-overlapping routes and connects networks, not a single service.

options.text: Publish the service on the internet behind the NLB with TLS and an allowlist of customer IP addresses.
options.why: Encrypted, but the service is internet-facing and depends on customer IPs staying stable.

options.text: Expose the NLB as a PrivateLink endpoint service and let customers create interface endpoints.
options.why: PrivateLink exposes only that service through endpoint ENIs in the customer's VPC; overlapping CIDRs don't matter because no routes are exchanged.

questions.explain: To share one service across accounts, especially with overlapping IP ranges, use PrivateLink. Peering and Transit Gateway connect whole networks and need unique CIDRs.

questions.stem: A clickstream data lake stores billions of small objects in S3 encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key. Every write and every Athena read calls AWS KMS, and KMS requests are now a large share of the monthly bill. The security team requires the same customer managed key to remain in use. Which change reduces cost the MOST while meeting this requirement?

options.text: Switch the bucket to SSE-S3 encryption.
options.why: SSE-S3 has no KMS charges, but it drops the customer managed key that the security team requires.

options.text: Enable S3 Bucket Keys for SSE-KMS on the bucket.
options.why: A bucket-level key derived from the KMS key is reused for many objects, which cuts KMS requests and their cost substantially with the same customer managed key.

options.text: Switch to client-side encryption with a data key cached in each producer.
options.why: It reduces KMS calls but requires changes in every producer and consumer, which costs far more effort.

options.text: Use an AWS managed key (aws/s3) instead of the customer managed key.
options.why: AWS managed keys still incur KMS requests and don't meet the requirement to keep the customer managed key.

questions.explain: S3 Bucket Keys are the standard fix for SSE-KMS request costs at high object counts. They keep the same KMS key and audit trail while cutting calls to KMS.

questions.stem: A broadcaster opened its AWS account this year and is closing a data center. It must move 1.2 PB of archived video from on-premises NAS to Amazon S3 within 6 weeks. The data center's 500 Mbps internet link is also used for daily operations, and its colocation provider is an AWS Direct Connect Partner. Which solution meets the deadline?

options.text: Use AWS DataSync over the existing internet connection.
options.why: DataSync is the right tool, but 1.2 PB over a shared 500 Mbps link takes well over 200 days, far beyond the deadline over the link that is available.

options.text: Order AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices, load them on site, and ship them back for import into S3.
options.why: This was the classic offline answer, but AWS closed Snowball Edge to new customers on 7 November 2025, so a company whose AWS account is new cannot order the devices.

options.text: Have the colocation provider, an AWS Direct Connect Partner, provision a 10 Gbps hosted connection, and run several AWS DataSync agents in parallel over it.
options.why: A hosted connection from a partner already in the facility is provisioned in days, and 10 Gbps carries the data well inside the deadline while DataSync handles parallelism, retries and integrity checks.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and upload with multipart uploads from the NAS.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration improves long-distance paths through edge locations, but it cannot exceed the capacity of the site's own internet link.

questions.explain: Start with arithmetic: data size divided by usable bandwidth, compared with the deadline. If the current link is too slow, add network capacity that can be provisioned in time (a hosted Direct Connect connection from a partner) and move the data with DataSync. Older material answers 'ship Snow Family devices'; since November 2025 new customers cannot order them, so expect network-based answers, and still read each scenario's constraints.

questions.stem: A film studio stores final master files in an S3 bucket in us-west-2. Its DR plan, agreed with distributors, says a copy of every new master must exist in eu-west-1 within 15 minutes of upload, and the company needs metrics and alerts when that target is missed. Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in eu-west-1 with S3 Replication Time Control enabled.
options.why: Replication Time Control is designed to replicate most objects within seconds and 99.9% within 15 minutes, and it publishes metrics and events for objects that miss it.

options.text: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication without additional options.
options.why: Standard CRR usually replicates quickly but has no time guarantee and no missed-threshold notifications.

options.text: Run a scheduled S3 Batch Operations job every 15 minutes that copies new objects.
options.why: Batch Operations works on manifests and is meant for bulk jobs, not continuous, time-bound replication.

options.text: Run an AWS DataSync task between the two buckets every hour with verification of transferred data turned on.
options.why: An hourly schedule cannot meet a 15-minute target, and it gives no per-object replication metrics.

questions.explain: If a stem puts a time bound on S3 replication (a 15-minute SLA, compliance), the answer is Replication Time Control. Plain CRR is asynchronous with no guaranteed timing.

questions.stem: A media conglomerate has 30 accounts that each run their own CloudFront distributions and ALBs for different magazine brands. The security team wants one baseline set of AWS WAF rules applied to every existing and new distribution and ALB across the organization, and it wants non-compliant resources fixed automatically. Which solution requires the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Firewall Manager with an AWS WAF policy scoped to the organization's accounts and resource types, with auto remediation enabled.
options.why: Firewall Manager applies WAF policies centrally across accounts, including new resources and accounts, and can remediate non-compliant ones.

options.text: Deploy the web ACL with AWS CloudFormation StackSets to every account and ask teams to associate it with their resources.
options.why: StackSets can deploy the web ACL, but the association to each new distribution and ALB still relies on every team.

options.text: Create one web ACL in the security account and share it to all accounts with AWS RAM.
options.why: WAF web ACLs are not shared through RAM this way, so teams could not attach the central ACL.

options.text: Run a scheduled Lambda function in every account that finds distributions and ALBs without the web ACL and associates the central web ACL with them.
options.why: It would work eventually, but it is custom code per account, which Firewall Manager replaces.

questions.explain: For security rules that must follow resources across an organization (WAF, Shield Advanced, security groups, Network Firewall), use Firewall Manager. It handles new accounts and resources and can remediate.
